Mr. Chairman, the committee has listened with interest, I know, to the comprehensive statement of the minister on this extremely important matter. As I rise to speak at this time I do not feel that I shall be able to cover on this occasion all the points he has raised or indeed all the points that I may wish to deal with. As I will not myself be able to be here at eight o'clock, I shall make some preliminary observations now and perhaps will have an opportunity later of contributing to the discussion. Particularly, Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to repeat-and I am sure the committee does not wish to hear-observations from this side of the chamber on the general economic and trade picture of the country, a subject which was rather exhaustively covered by the budget debate. However, the minister has given an optimistic picture of the economic and trade situation. He has shown that the economy, during the year he covered in his statement, has given indications of strength, recovery and resilience and that there has been economic improvement both nationally and internationally. Certainly for Canada the two things go together.
Naturally we on this side of the chamber as Canadians welcome any indication of this strenghtening of the economic and trade situation in the country. We must welcome every move that is being made in that direction. As I have said, the minister has given an optimistic picture. It is an optimism which is based on the favourable evidence that he has been able to muster, a great deal of which appears in the annual report. He has mentioned how things like consumer spending and inventory accumulation held up and have made their contribution to that which he has called national expansion but which I think more realistically could be termed national recovery from recession. Expansion has not taken place but recovery has to some extent taken place. Of course, recovery is a necessary foundation, I admit, if expansion is to take place.
On the basis of the evidence that he has submitted the minister talks about national

Supply-Trade and Commerce expansion and compares what he calls international expansion with what has happened in the years prior to 1958. He refers then to the world recession from which we are nationally recovering and expanding. In his statement he has made it quite clear that in this recovery which we must all hope will be the foundation for expansion, nevertheless our dependence on international developments is as great as it ever has been. We cannot escape that particular hostage which we in this country have given to fortune. In that dependence on international conditions it is clearer than ever that our economic and trade relationship with the United States plays a most vital part. If this country has ever been economically dependent on the United States and United States conditions-and of course it has always been dependent to some extent-I suggest that dependence now-and I think the figures will show this, notwithstanding the varied nature of our international trade-is perhaps greater than it has been at any other time.
I do not know how we will escape this. I am not asking at this stage whether it is desirable or not to escape it, but I know that the minister and his colleagues in former years pointed out in no uncertain terms and with great vehemence the danger to Canada because of this economic dependence. It was a danger to Canada's political and national development generally because of the undue importance of our commercial and trade relationships with one country, a country so close to us in every way as is the United States.
We now have all the detailed information concerning the Canadian balance of international payments for the first quarter of 1959, and the minister has made reference to it in his statement. That information reveals that while there are forces of recovery at work, as I have mentioned, there are also weak points in the economy. There are some dangers and difficulties ahead, and just as the minister has emphasized the bright side of the picture, it is our right and our duty to point out some of the difficulties and dangers which, if they are not met and dealt with in so far as any national government can do so, will impede and hinder these forces of recovery which are at work.
A dominion bureau of statistics publication of June 18, 1959, the Daily Bulletin of that date, gives some indication of the nature of these difficulties and dangers, and what I mean when I talk about the serious side of the economic situation. Here are some of the headlines from that particular bulletin for the first quarter of 1959. We had during that quarter a current deficit of $450 million in


goods and services with other countries, compared with $282 million and $427 million, respectively, for the first quarters of 1958 and 1957. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, the current deficit is the highest in our history for this particular period of the year. I recall what my hon. friends opposite used to say about deficits of this kind and the threat that they involved to our economy and stability.
During this period there was a rise of nine per cent in the value of merchandise imports, to which the minister has given his own interpretation, which along with a slight drop, a very slight drop, in the export total had the effect of producing a trade deficit of $188 million in the first quarter of 1959, compared with $63 million deficit in 1958. It is just about three times the deficit for the same period last year. The deficit from non-merchandise transactions continued to rise and reached $262 million, compared with $219 million in 1958, $201 million in 1957, and $176 million in 1956.
The current account deficit with the United States-and we used to hear so much about the danger to this country from increasing deficits with the United States-rose from $320 million in 1958 to $428 million in 1959; but at the same time the surplus with the United Kingdom continued at about $12 million. This deficit was compensated, as indeed it had been compensated in the past when it occurred, by a net movement of foreign capital into Canada, the main supplier being the United States of America. We have been informed more than once in the past of the difficulties which involve our country in this type of influx of capital to such a great extent from one source, the United States of America.
Mr. Chairman, last year I recall the minister making quite a virtue out of the fact that the deficit with the United States had been reduced. We pointed out to the minister at that time that indeed that was the case, but it was the case because the imports had gone down faster than the exports, and that was not the right way to reduce a deficit. Nevertheless the minister felt that was an encouraging feature in the situation, the reduction of the deficit. This year the minister admits, of course, that the deficit with the United States has increased, but he gets a different kind of encouragement out of that. The minister says that it is due to the fact that business expansion has developed and we are importing more than we used to from the United States, and if the deficit has increased it is encouraging because of the nature of the increase. In other words, it is impossible to make the minister anything but

optimistic with regard to trade figures. If the deficit is reduced it is a virtue; if it is increased it is a virtue.
Here is another bureau of statistics Daily Bulletin, dated June 23 which gives detailed information on imports during the first quarter of 1959 and which has a bearing on some of these developments which I have mentioned. Let us see what these figures show. The United States and the United Kingdom were the respective sources of 71.8 per cent and 8.8 per cent of Canadian imports during that first quarter. There is certainly no indication of any trade diversion in those figures. In relation to that famous diversion proposal or policy about which we used to hear so much, but not so much now, it is interesting to note the following changes in our import trade in 1959 as compared with 1958.
The minister said a few minutes ago, if I recollect it correctly, that the increase in our imports was spread over the whole field of foreign trade. But the figures in the report to which I am referring do not indicate that, because imports from the United States during this period rose by almost four per cent while imports from the United Kingdom-and remember it was the policy of the government to divert imports from the United States to the United Kingdom-during this same period declined by about six per cent. Therefore it does not seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that this policy of trade diversion is working out very successfully. As I have already said in the house, it seems to me to be working in reverse.
I wonder what there is to show for this trade mission of a year and a half ago to the United Kingdom. What is there to show for this pilgrimage to the United Kingdom which was conducted with so much publicity and great expense, the purpose of which was to increase British exports to Canada, or to increase our imports from the United Kingdom, and reduce them from the United States? It is true that imports from the commonwealth exclusive of the United Kingdom did rise by about five per cent. It is also true that our imports from Europe rose by more than 22 per cent, and from Latin America by three per cent. But the real diversion has not been the diversion we heard so much about a year and a half ago or so; it has been the opposite to that. We are importing less from the United Kingdom and more from the United States.
Let us look at the figures for exports about which the hon. gentleman had something to say. The same dominion bureau of statistics bulletin published on June 19 contains information on our export trade in May and for the first five months of 1959. The minister 66968-9-329i
Supply-Trade and Commerce maintained that our export trade in a period of what he called world recession had held up remarkably well in 1958. That is true in the sense that the figures were just about the same. There was a very slight decrease, but the figures were just about the same as they were a year before. But that is not good enough for a country such as Canada which depends so much on the export trade. Exports must increase every year or we are going to be in trouble in this country, and the nature of our export trade in 1958 shows that we would have been in serious trouble at that time had it not been for three things. The development of our uranium exports under an agreement concluded in 1956 to the point where uranium is now our most important mineral export figures for which this year may reach $300 million, was one thing that held our exports up. Exports of cattle were something else, and our exports of aircraft under NATO arrangements and under the Colombo plan, which were not strictly speaking exports but were gifts or transfers, also helped. Had it not been for these particular items we would have been in a serious situation last year with regard to exports.
In comparison with last year, when there was no increase over 1957, our exports in May were down by more than 10 per cent and they declined by about 3 per cent in the first five months. This is partly explained, as I think the minister mentioned, by the fact that last year there were exceptionally large deliveries of aircraft to Germany and a rather high volume of financed exports but, nevertheless, it represents a situation which must cause a certain anxiety, whatever the reason may be.
Both in May and during the first five months our exports to the United States increased, but our exports to the rest of the world, including the United Kingdom, declined. As a result, in the first five months of 1958, 58.1 per cent of our exports went to the United States as compared to 62.5 per cent in 1959. Our eggs are more and more concentrated in only one basket, this United States basket, and the danger of this kind of concentration should be very apparent to members of the government who talked so much about it when they were on this side of the house.
These statistics which I have quoted-and they are the latest available-show that we are now experiencing the highest deficit in goods and services with other countries in our history, and that our export trade on the basis of the first five months is declining. We join the minister in the hope that that decline will be arrested during the rest of the year, but at the present time we are

Supply-Trade and Commerce faced with this decline and we are becoming more and more dependent on the United States with respect to our trade arrangements. Our imports are rapidly increasing and that increase comes from all countries in the world except the United Kingdom, but again mainly from the United States. Our net imports of capital are also increasing, and I suggest the committee will want to give serious attention to the policy implications of this particular picture, and we shall want to hear more from the minister as this discussion goes on about the trade policy of the government in this respect.
Perhaps at this time I might mention one thing which, as the minister knows, is a matter of immediate and great importance, and I have asked him a good many questions about it in the house. In the light of these decreasing figures for exports it becomes all the more important-indeed, it becomes a matter of the most vital significance-to make the necessary arrangements with the United States government to continue its imports of uranium from Canada once the present treaty arrangement lapses. The minister has been to Washington to discuss this matter with the United States government. He spent a day there a couple of months ago, I think, but I suggest to him that the importance of this matter justifies the most formal and the most impressive representations that can be made to the United States government at the highest possible level.
I am very familiar with the background of this particular arrangement because I had something to do with its negotiation, and I remember that at that time the United States said: "Go ahead and develop every pound of uranium you have in Canada; it is vital to our security and to the security of the free world and to your own security; commercial considerations must take second place; we need this; the supply is not equal to our demand; this is a matter of first importance, to develop these fields in Canada; we will help you; we will make this contract with you; we will do anything necessary; we will see that you get a good price for it, so go ahead."
Canadian producers went ahead and made a very good arrangement for the longest term possible, namely five years, with an option to continue this contract at the end of the five-year period. If it should happen- and I certainly hope it does not happen; it seems to me there is no reason why it should happen-at the end of this period that the United States authorities should come along and say: now we have a lot of uranium of our own-and they have got a lot of uranium- we have developed our own fields during


these five years; we have our own political problems and we have our own economic problems; we have had to take care of our own interests and our own producers; and while we have been very happy to have your uranium during the past five years we do not need it now, it would be an intolerable position and one that could not be accepted by any Canadian government.
Yet the time is coming when the Canadian producers will have to know whether in fact arrangements of this kind can be made to continue the conditions under which they are operating and I think it would be a great relief to them if they could be told before the end of this year. There have been suggestions made in the United States by officials-and I hope they are not well founded-that it may be difficult to continue the present arrangement with Canadian producers. I hope that not only will the government give this matter the attention it deserves on the highest diplomatic level but that before long it will be able to make an announcement that a specific arrangement has been made with the United States. If continental defence means anything at all-* and, of course, it does mean something-it means that some consideration has to be given to the economic and industrial aspects of defence on a continental basis as well as to the strategic aspect and if there was ever an important economic and industrial aspect of defence it is the supply of uranium for defence purposes.
There is no doubt in my mind that the long term prospects for uranium production in Canada are good, and I think this will be the view of all hon. members. The world is going to need this commodity. But there may be a difficult period between the end of this contract and the development of new uses for uranium for industrial purposes, a period which would be very difficult indeed if the United States decided not to take into full consideration the position of Canadian producers. I sincerely hope that this will not happen and I certainly hope it will be a major policy of the government to see that it does not happen because it involves export trade this year, as I have said, of some $300 million.
It is not possible, Mr. Chairman, to talk about the importance of our export trade in any of its aspects without at the same time referring to our import policies because we are not going to be able to develop our export trade unless we can make satisfactory arrangements with our customers for a reasonable import of goods from those countries into Canada. I thought of this the other day when the Minister of Finance

made an announcement regarding a voluntary arrangement which had been made with the Japanese government for the reduction of certain imports into this country from Japan. I certainly appreciate the problem involved in the importing into this country of goods with which it is difficult, if not impossible, for Canadian producers to compete because of the conditions under which these goods are manufactured in the country of origin. When competition is not fair, then, of course, the government has to take steps to meet unfairness of competition and protect and help Canadian producers.
But I should like to point out that we shall have to be especially careful in the steps we take in respect of a customer which already buys three or four times as much from Canada as it sells to Canada. I do not have the exact figures but I think it is about that proportion. I am talking about Japan now. The Toronto Globe and Mail will not be accused of being a paper which is unfair to our manufacturers or unduly starry-eyed about free trade, and in the issue of June 22 it had this to say in an editorial:
Considering the fact that Japan buys far more from Canada than it sells to Canada, the Japanese government is most obliging when it agrees, at the Canadian government's request, to curtail Japanese exports to Canada.
The editorial goes on to say:
The steps taken to restrict imports will undoubtedly help those industries which have been hurt by them, and in that respect the government's policy will reach its goal. But it is a very limited role, and one which in being achieved may do considerably more harm than good. There is much more to this question than mere protectionism.
The final paragraph reads in part as follows:
We are more concerned, apparently, with the effect on our domestic producers of imported Japanese underwear than with the catastrophe looming over the Pacific horizon.
What was meant by that, and it is a very good illustration of the interrelation of politics and economics, was that if Japan is driven from or discouraged from entering the markets of the west she will find her own markets on the continent of China because there will be no alternative, and if Japan begins to build up a trading relationship with continental China because she is denied it by the west that relationship may have political results which would be very unfortunate indeed for the west.
The minister had something to say about the development of the European common market, the development toward European integration. I was glad he spoke about this because I do not know of anything more important that has taken place in the economic and, indeed, perhaps almost in the political
Supply-Trade and Commerce sphere at the present time. It is true that in the last dozen years we in this country and other free governments have worked out our multilateral trading relationships quite satisfactorily and on the whole successfully through GATT, and I think GATT has performed a most useful function in those years in the removal of restrictions and the building up of multilateral relationships.
But while GATT in recent years has been retained as a general framework, the conditions under which GATT was formed in the earlier years are changing and I think it is becoming more and more apparent now that perhaps a new look will have to be taken at this whole idea of international trade and the basis on which it should rest. The practical operation of GATT has become increasingly altered by the domestic policies of many countries and many of those countries who are members of GATT and who pay lip service to its arrangements are beginning- some of them have more than begun-to base their trading policies on more restrictive arrangements than those of GATT.
The sterling area has been maintained as an important trading group. The United States continues to be a vast and relatively isolated trading area. The Sino-soviet bloc is rapidly expanding as a trading area and the European common market, which was not considered when GATT was formed, is becoming a reality, a reality which I think on more than economic grounds we should welcome provided it is brought about in the right way.
Then, only recently the Latin American countries have initiated discussions about the possibility of forming some kind of economic union of Latin America, and world trade therefore is increasingly becoming dominated by economic giants and economic trading blocs. In the intermediate period at least we may expect a further extension of extranational systems of pooled currencies, customs unions and large scale bilateralism and perhaps even a more limited application rather than a wider application of the multilateralism as envisaged in GATT.
No country stands to be affected more by this development than Canada. It is still, of course, too early to say what will happen to world trade within this new context and to those countries like Canada whose prosperity, whose independence, whose economic stability, depend to such a large extent on an expanding multilateralism. This contrary evolution, presents serious potential dangers which should be considered most carefully by any Canadian government.
For instance, the establishment of a common market in Europe, to which the minister has made reference, will undoubtedly produce benefits both economic and political, I

Supply-Trade and Commerce hope, but it may also bring new difficulties for world trade and even for the maintenance of the western alliance. What I mean when I say that is simply this. If this European movement takes place without some kind of association with North America we will have an economic trading area in Europe increasingly divorced from a North American trading area, let us say at present from the United States. If that happens the effect will be political as well as economic on the Atlantic alliance, and if we do have this kind of European development which has not been able to make arrangements with the United States, what is the position of Canada going to be at a time when the continental aspects of security are also becoming increasingly important in the United States as opposed to the Atlantic aspects? If somehow the European development cannot become an Atlantic development, and I have said this many times, Canada will probably have to make one of the most difficult choices in her history and, as I ventured to say this morning, not only is this important for Canada politically but it is going to be very important for Canada economically because this new European development promises to become one of the major trading areas in the world. It is already increasing its percentage of world trade while North America's percentage is going down.
Because of the memories, experience, devastation, destruction, poverty and distress after the war, we are accustomed to think of Europe as still being a kind of distressed area. Perhaps that is too complacent a view, as the figures which I put on the record this morning would seem to indicate. Therefore I suggest that there can be no more important aspect of trade policy at the present time than the conversion of the European free trade area into an Atlantic freer trade area. The common market has begun to work out its own difficulties but the European free trade area, which it was hoped would evolve from the common market, is not making very much progress.
But, as the minister pointed out in his statement, those countries which are now in Europe outside the common market are beginning to consider forming another European common market. In the discussions which have just been held in the last few weeks-I think they were held in Stockholm-there was a good deal of support given to the idea of building up this other European area, which would include the United Kingdom if the present common market could not be expanded into a free trade area. If this is done,
[Mr. Pearson.l

what will be the relationship of the United Kingdom in that market to her commonwealth trading relationships?
Perhaps the minister has noticed this, as I have, in reading British weeklies such as the Economist and the Times. High officials of the British government are now willing to consider the position of the United Kingdom in that kind of European organization and the relationship of that position to their commonwealth trading obligations. Therefore, this is a matter not only of economics but of very considerable political importance. Also, Mr. Chairman, if this European movement is developed, and if it develops in the right way through the removal of trade barriers against those outside the arrangement, then surely it is not too soon for the Canadian government perhaps to take the lead in trying to work out arrangement by which the United States and Canada can be associated with these developments.
You have the European common market. They are now discussing over there a second common market which might join the other into a European free trade area. The time has come to try to expand the discussion at least of these arrangements to an Atlantic basis. And if, as we are so often told these days, the real problem ahead of us in our relations with the countries behind the iron curtain, the Sino-soviet bloc, is going to be more economic than political, if the danger to us is economic as much as it is political, then on political as well as on economic grounds it becomes a matter of the first importance to build up the European into the Atlantic area.
There are some other things I should like to talk about arising out of the minister's statement, but perhaps, since it is almost six o'clock, I will reserve my observations on this until a later stage in the debate.

Mr. Chairman, there is an unfortunate circumstance in connection with the discussion of these estimates that perhaps is just one of those things that nothing can be done about at this stage and it is this. The committee concerned with the operations of the wheat board and the board of grain commissioners reports is sitting at the same time as the committee of the whole house is discussing these estimates. It means a duplication of demands on the same members who are interested in being in both places at the same time. I would hope that another year it will be possible to arrange the programming of the committee's sittings and of the sittings of the committee of the whole house on the estimates a little more

conveniently so that that can be avoided. I know the difficulties this particular year in detailing the arrangements and I am therefore not objecting to the agriculture committee sitting today while these estimates are before the house.
There are many general remarks which could be made because the subject of trade is so wide ranging and perhaps if I sought to deal with one or two of the matters of policy on which we are seeking to get clarification at this stage of the estimates that is on the first item of the department's estimates, it would be a more orderly way of proceeding.
I should like to raise for further discussion from the minister the subject of trade with the West Indies; that is, something fuller by way of report as to what progress has been made in the development of the trade relationship with the West Indies area since the estimates were before the committee one year ago. In particular, I should like the minister to elaborate on our relative position in that market. I fear that in the development of the federation and the economic development going on in that area, which we hope will continue and accelerate, Canada may be in danger of not holding its relative position and developing the potential of trade in that area to its maximum possibilities.
The trade in that area is particularly important to Canada to a degree more than is indicated in terms of dollars because of the nature of the products which we exchange; that is the products we import from that country seem to supplement the products we produce here to a greater degree than is true of most of the trading areas.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, another
reason why the trade with the West Indies has extraordinary significance for Canada beyond the number of dollars indicated in the figures, important as that aspect of it is, is that the products the West Indies take from Canada come largely from the Atlantic region where the problem of finding markets for their output is undoubtedly more severe than in many other parts of the country. This trade, therefore, has abnormal significance to that area.
There is a great deal of capital development going on in the West Indies and I have the impression-I should like the minister to comment on this-that the capital development
Supply-Trade and Commerce going on as a result of enterprise supplied from outside the area is not being contributed to by Canada to as large an extent as we would wish. I believe that some of our competitors in that market may be supplying a larger porportion of the capital development than their trade with the area would warrant. If we are not supplying our proportionate part, this would ultimately tend to result in a lessening of our trade with the area, that is a lessening of our proportion of the trade with the area.
I dealt with this subject at some length a year ago on a private member's motion which I put on the order paper. At that time I indicated my criticism of the government for having disposed of the Canadian National steamships and, in that way, having impaired shipping to the area at a time when the federation was just in the process of being formed. I thought that was a wrong action for the government to have taken, although I was quite willing to concede that there was some difficulty in carrying on that shipping and that a subsidy was required. I then went on to deal with trade agreements and tariff matters. I fear that the tariff aspect of that discussion became overdeveloped because tariffs are not the main barriers to trade with the area. The tariffs are relatively low. The difficulties seem to arise from other sources, one of them of course being that the federated area has no customs union within itself. There are different duties applicable to each part. In addition, they do not have control of their own currency and this makes things more difficult.
I should like to hear the minister's report on any discussions he has had with the United Kingdom on the subject of trade with the West Indies, and particularly the currency aspect of the matter. When one considers what a tremendous achievement the development of Canada's own currency was some 100 years ago one can fully appreciate that it is a somewhat restricting force when an area like the West Indies does not have control over its own currency. I do not want to discuss matters that are internal to that area and are not our concern here, but I do hope that the area is able to solve these problems that are peculiarly within its own control or should be within its own control in a way that will help them develop their economy. I hope when that comes along we will be able to develop our trade with the area to our mutual advantage. I am one of those who attaches a great deal of importance to the control of the currency in the area so far as it affects our trading relations. I would hope that the minister would take every proper opportunity he can to

Supply-Trade and Commerce discuss this aspect of trade relations, particularly with the United Kingdom government, to the end that we can enlarge the volume of trade in that part of the world.
Another matter with which I wanted to deal at this stage of the estimates is our trade with Japan. The trade figures, as I have them here, show the imports from Japan in 1957 at $61,604,000 and the exports from Canada to Japan in that year at $139,151,000; in 1958, imports from Japan, $70,215,000; exports to Japan, $104,890,000; for the first three months of the current year imports from Japan amounted to $21,468,000 and exports for that period amounted to $27,175,000. It is interesting that the main export seems to be barley, as I recall. I believe in the year 1958 the barley exports to Japan amounted to something of the order of $62 million in value, a very large part of the total exports. I should think that the members from western Canada would be particularly interested in this particular trade with Japan.
The Minister of Finance made an announcement to the house on June 19 concerning the suspension of certain exports from Japan to Canada. His statement is found at page 4927 of Hansard of that date. I shall not read it, but there is a sentence or two which might help me make my point. The minister was referring to the representations made to the Canadian government by certain manufacturers in Canada on the subject of the damage being done to their industries by imports from Japan. I am very well aware of that and I do not wish anything in my remarks to underestimate the importance of looking after that matter.
The point I want to discuss is that the minister went on then to say that the Canadian government, following these representations from the Canadian manufacturers, had made representations to the Japanese government. I will quote him precisely as follows:
Accordingly discussions were undertaken with the representatives of the Japanese government in Ottawa and Tokyo, in the course of which the views of the Canadian government were communicated to them. Within recent days I have held discussions with the Japanese ambassador which gave me the opportunity to state the Canadian position. This meeting was followed up by meetings between senior officials of the Canadian government and representatives of the Japanese government.
We were informed only last night of the decision of the Japanese government respecting the suspension of the issuance of new export licences.
Then he goes on from there. What concerns me is this. The figures of trade with that area, and particularly our exports to Japan, show that the exports are very much larger than our imports from Japan. There is a very substantial imbalance of trade between


our country and Japan. They show further that our exports to Japan decreased sharply from 1957 when they were some $139 million in value to 1958 when they dropped to $104 million in value. The first thing I should like the minister to do is to explain that drop in our exports to Japan. I suspect that one of the factors-and I think he will agree with this statement-was the shortage of dollars that the Japanese had with which to buy our goods. That factor poses a real problem because, as our western friends will be very quick to remind us, it is extremely important that we retain that market for the export of the many products we ship there. I took barley by way of illustration for Japan is much our biggest market for barley. I should therefore like the minister to deal with that problem.
Then I want the minister to deal more fully with the whole subject. The Minister of Finance, in making the announcement to the house, very appropriately confined himself to a statement of the bare facts but I should like the minister to elaborate on this somewhat difficult subject very fully so that we will know what the policy of the government is with respect to the trade in this particular area.
I have spoken only of the trade significance of it. My leader this afternoon, in speaking about this same subject, made reference to other aspects of the matter that are of tremendous importance to the welfare of this country and to our future in this country, aspects that are even more important than the trade aspect. However, I want to confine my remarks at the moment to the trade aspect.
This statement of the Minister of Finance is fairly factual and fairly blunt, if I may say so. I should like to know from the minister just what representations were made to the Japanese government. This statement, as it stands in Hansard, almost looks as though fairly firm pressure was applied or fairly firm representations were made as to what would be done. My point in raising that matter is this. I hope that we are not embarking on any program of undue force or improper force, if I may use that term, in our position in these matters. While I believe in great firmness, I do not believe in threats of any kind or anything of that nature. I am not saying that the statement of the Minister of Finance contained that implication but I am saying that the subject requires further elaboration and development.
Then the matter of the treaty with Japan, the rights we have under the treaty and so on, should be developed. There is, of course, the whole aspect of the matter of protecting our industries in Canada that may be unduly

hurt by products coming in that are priced below what is a fair and reasonable price and so on. I am not unmindful of that problem in discussing the trade aspect of the matter but it is a very severe thing to have exports to one country drop by a third in one year. There probably is some explanation for this but as the figures stand, that is what they show. It is something that I hope the government will keep in mind and that I hope the minister will deal with at some length.
Then there is one other matter with which I should like to deal. The minister this afternoon in his statement, as I recall it, in speaking about the * expansion of the economy, of the increase in imports this current year, about exports and the deficit on merchant trade being wider than it was last year as I noted his remarks, said this among other things:
Looking at shifts in the geographic pattern of Canada's trade so far this year, it is noteworthy that sales to the United States have been increasing. On the other hand, the increase in Canada's imports has been shared by all major trading areas.
What I should like him to clarify a bit for me is this. The figures of sales to the United States, as I have them, show that there was a decline of some $425 million in exports to that country last year and that exports to that country are up some $30 million in the first four months of this current year but that in the first three months of the current year they were down. I think the figures support this statement. I have the statistical summaries here if the minister wants them but I think they support that statement. The May figure is not distributed yet, but from what the minister says I assume it may also be up. The point I want to make on that matter is this. If the minister is taking a one-month period only as the factor to indicate a change in direction or trend, his statement is surely straining the desire to be optimistic a bit too far. If you have three months in which there is a decline in the trade and then in the fourth month you have an increase, surely it is hardly a fair way in which to leave the matter just to say that sales to the United States have been increasing. It is true as far as it goes if you take last month as an example, but surely that is not a fair way of presenting trade figures to the house. I for one certainly do not want to read into any such short term figures as that a long term trend. I think it is just not a realistic way in which to handle this subject, because exports can vary quite sharply from month to month as the minister well knows. If you pick out any one month, I suppose you could prove almost anything
Supply-Trade and Commerce from the statistics. I wish the minister would elaborate a bit more on that point. Then in the next sentence he went on to say this:
On the other hand, the increase in Canada's imports has been shared by all major trading areas.
I have the figures for the imports from the United Kingdom, a very important customer indeed. As I read the figures for 1957 our imports for consumption from the United Kingdom amounted to $521,957,000 and for 1958, $526,650,000 or in other words an increase in imports from the United Kingdom of $5 million in the year 1958 over the year 1957. But when I come to the year 1959 I find that the imports from the United Kingdom for the first three months of 1958 had been some $116,170,000 in value and for the first three months of 1959, some $108,872,000. In other words, there is a decline in imports in the first quarter of this year over the comparable period for last year of some $7.4 million or something of that order. On the other hand, the statement that the increase in Canada's imports has been shared by all major trading areas seems to require some further explanation, because the United Kingdom is a very important trading area and it is not sufficient to have a generalization like that when we remember that one of the problems in trade with the United Kingdom is that we have a substantial surplus of exports over imports from that country. In addition, and I think this is fair comment, the minister and his colleagues made a great deal of how they were going to lessen that differential in trade with the United Kingdom; they talked a great deal about that. They were going to divert some of the imports from the United States to the United Kingdom, and so on. But that problem has not been met, and indeed any figures available, for example the figures used some months ago when the government talked about how they had succeeded in effecting that situation, when analysed show that what happened was a lessening of the differential in trade by reduced exports from Canada to the United Kingdom. Therefore I would like to have that item explained a little more fully.
Then there is a further matter I would like to speak about, and that is the whole problem of the export of farm surpluses as it relates to trade. In other words, I am not seeking to reopen the discussion we had with the Minister of Agriculture about farm incomes and that sort of thing. What I want to deal with tonight are the implications of that policy carried out by the government of disposing of farm surpluses at considerably below their cost; the taxpayers buy them from the farmers and then they are sold in the export

Supply-Trade and Commerce market at a very much lower price. It will be recalled that on March 6 of this year, as appears at page 1720 of Hansard, I asked a question about the sale of eggs to Venezuela by the Canadian government since December 1, 1958, their price, and so on. The answer I received, which I can summarize, shows that the Canadian government was adopting a policy of buying eggs at 44 cents per dozen, grade A large, Montreal, and had sold these eggs, in this particular case to Venezuela, at from 5 cents to 16 cents per dozen below that price, and there may have been additional costs involved too. That will indicate-
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.
Has the hon. member any proof that they were grade A eggs which were being sold?

I only have the statement of the Minister of Agriculture. He stated that was the basis of the price paid, and I would not want to quarrel with the word of the Minister of Agriculture on this occasion. I certainly do not think it would be fitting for me to do so; the hon. member may do so if he wishes.
Then on April 13 I asked a further question on this same subject, which appears at page 2652 of Hansard. The question concerned certain agricultural products being purchased by the government and sold abroad. I will just pick out one or two of the items to illustrate my point. We were buying powdered skim milk at a price up to May 1, 1958- perhaps I should give the figures for the whole period-of from 12 cents to 17 cents per pound and we were selling that product to a great number of countries at as low as 3.15 cents per pound; in other words, something of the order of a quarter of the price we paid for it. That sale was presumably ,on a feed basis, though the answer does not say so in so many words. However, the point I want to make here is this, that we have embarked upon a policy of using the public -revenues of this country to buy these farm products and then to sell them on the foreign markets at very much below the cost to the taxpayers.
Mr. Chairman, there are two or three implications of that, and I can find no statement of policy from the government on the trade aspects of the subject. It must be pointed cut that in shipping products like this to countries like Denmark, we are in fact subsidizing competitors in certain of the other markets of the world to the detriment of our own product. We have lost some of the markets in the United Kingdom for agricultural

products because our prices are already too high. But the government is now subsidizing a competitor who has taken over most of the market, or a large part of it to compete against our product, our product being, as I say, already too highly priced. It seems to me that is not a reasonable way of meeting the difficulty which we have in Canada of keeping the farmers' incomes sufficiently high. This so-called solution is not a solution at all.

Mr, Chairman, we have been reminded that Canada is dependent on foreign trade to perhaps a greater degree than any other nation. I have seen figures which state that one job out of every five is dependent on foreign trade. As far as British Columbia is concerned, I believe the figure would be one out of four, and this figure would be higher for the prairie provinces. So the economy of western Canada is even more dependent upon export trade than that of eastern Canada.
We are particularly interested in promoting an increased trade with the United Kingdom, because the products of western Canada are more or less complementary to products produced in the United States. The United States market represents a large and most important market to us but it represents products which the United States domestic producer can also produce and with whom we must compete to sell in that market. The sterling area, however, represents not a limitless market but a market which could be developed to a far higher degree than it is today if our trade pattern could be so increased or if our trade volume between the sterling area and Canada could be increased so that we could take advantage of that market.
The British Columbia lumber manufacturers association, the British Columbia fisheries council-all our primary producers- have made numerous representations along these lines. We believe more could be done in that way to promote the sale of United Kingdom products in Canada. For instance, I happen to know that in the engineering field a British manufacturer who wishes to enter this market is told that service must be of such and such a standard, that his design must be in conformity with the United States standards in the form of screw threads, pipe sizes and so on and that there must be good delivery. I should like the committee to know that many a United Kingdom manufacturer has come over to this country and been able to fulfil all those requirements yet he still does not get

any business even with a low price because our technical people know the United States product and they do not know the United Kingdom product.
It will be said that this is a matter of salesmanship, and it is, but even after the manufacturer has gone to a lot of expense and trouble he is still in an inferior position visa-vis his United States competition because they are entrenched in the market, their product has been accepted and there is a bias toward that product in many cases because of the control of the company and the policy of that particular company. I know of many instances where equivalent United Kingdom producers were low bidders but because instructions had been received by the firm concerned that they were not to buy that equipment, the bid was not accepted. I think the same process takes place, though not as a result of instructions, with regard to government purchases because I know of examples where, because the engineers in the field were familiar with the United States product, that product has been supplied for some reason or another in place of a competing United Kingdom product even though the United Kingdom product has been acceptable and in use in this country for a good many years. So I say that a program of education is required in the lower echelon of even our own civil service in the way of training to carry out the policy of the government in achieving a widely diversified and multi-lateral trading program.
I have here some newspaper clippings which might illustrate some of the troubles we run into, because these clippings have to do with selling in the United States and buying from the United States.
The second major market is the United Kingdom but I have a clipping from the Vancouver Province of May 12 in which it states "Low Canadian Tender Shakes U.S. Bidders" and continues:
The offer of a Canadian firm to build eight hydraulic turbines for the Big Bend dam in South Dakota for 30 per cent less than the lowest U.S. bidder has American electrical industry leaders deeply concerned.
Now the "Buy American" act does allow United States firms a 12 per cent price advantage over their competition, but the thing that shook the United States firms was the fact that these turbines were not going to be made in Switzerland or the United Kingdom but in Canada where our manufacturing costs are comparable with those in the United States and it could not be claimed that this price advantage would be a product of low wages.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
And then in the Financial Post of May 16 under the heading "Inglis Expects Big U.S. Order", one paragraph says:
A Liberal member said in Ottawa this week that the bid had been rejected, and suggested that the U.S. had violated its production-sharing arrangements with Canada.
Then on May 30 there is a long story on the same subject. As far as I know, a decision has not yet been made but it is the office of civilian and defence mobilization which will be making the decision on this matter and the only reason this office has authority to reject a low bid would be in the interest of national security.
The other clipping I have is from the Globe and Mail of June 2 and it is headed: "Mayor Irked but TTC Sticks to U.S.-Made Buses". This article says that the TTC bought General Motors buses at a much higher price than Canadian buses because it believed they were better buses and felt they would be better value. The moral of this story, to me, is this. We are a small industrial nation with a wide open free market here, yet the industrial giant of the world, the United States, must have protection against us. I think there is a job to be done in opening up the United States market, not just for Canadian primary products and semi-processed goods such as pulp, minerals, asbestos and newsprint, but for our manufactured goods. I suggest that some of the troubles which our manufacturers have in reaching the United States market are artificial ones such as a hodgepodge of U.S. customs regulations particularly against manufactured goods. Everybody remembers the case of the ping pong balls being classified as ammunition, but the fact is that the Canadian exporter to the U.S. is under a liability which may extend up to seven years for any extra duty which may be suffered from reclassification. I believe it is possible for our manufacturers to enter the United States market to a far greater degree if they are given the opportunity.
Then, of course, there is the final barrier in that so much of our manufacturing industry is controlled from the United States and they are not going to have their Canadian subsidiaries competing with their own plants within the United States. But there is a United States market there which can be developed and which will help to make that bigger trade pie we are trying to develop by means of greater imports from the United Kingdom and greater exports to that country, and greater sales to the United States because, after all, we are running a deficit with the United States of about $1 billion a year and there is certainly room

Supply-Trade and Commerce in that area for the United States to buy much more from us. Then, of course, there is our own Canadian market. I was interested in a paragraph in Industry, a publication put out I believe by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and in one paragraph it said:
In 1957, despite our position as one of the leading manufacturing nations of the world, we imported, fully finished manufactured goods to the tune of $262 for every man, woman and child in the country. By comparison the British figure was $48 and the U.S. a mere $28.
We have within our own country a large market which could be supplied by Canadian manufacturers at, I suggest, no increase in price to the Canadian consumer. I suggest we might improve our position by developing our own internal trade and also by widening the range of our multilateral trading program and, in that regard, devising some way of operating a massive export credit program for dealing with nations such as Brazil and other South American countries who operate almost on a barter basis.
I think we can continue to increase our trade and build it to the point where it will provide more employment and greater prosperity in the country than today.
With regard to the rather belittling attitude taken by the opposition as to our export trade last year when the level was just about the same as the preceding year, the highest figure on record, I was interested to note in a trade publication that United States export trade had fallen by some 12 per cent, I believe. Having in mind the comparison between the performance of Canada and that of the United States and the fact that we maintained an export volume equal to the highest level in the history of this country in a year of recession, I think this is a tribute to the work of the department and a tribute to the minister.

Mr. Chairman, the former minister of trade and commerce, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, led several delegations to various countries and with remarkable success. At the recent Atlantic congress held in London one of the major objectives of the NATO alliance was emphasized to be the promotion of trade within the European community. I wish to read a couple of paragraphs from one of the resolutions dealing with the subject of trade.
The aims and interests of the North Atlantic community will be best served by ensuring the maximum possible freedom of trade and stability of prices and exchanges. Governments should regard further progress toward freedom of trade and currencies as a major and urgent objective of economic policy. Governments, while recognizing that during this process they may have to resort to temporary expedience, should not take measures which involve a return to restrictionism.

The question I wish to ask the minister is this and I hope he will be able to hear me. Does the minister intend to visit the countries of the European community for the express purpose of stimulating trade with these countries and does the government intend to give consideration to a complete study of international trade? It appears to me that the government should regard further progress toward greater freedom of trade as a major and urgent objective of economic policy for the government of Canada. I sincerely trust that the minister will give due consideration to these proposals and that I will have an answer from him.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to the attention of the committee certain problems which vitally affect not only my own constituency of Saskatoon but also other centres in Canada which at present have similar problems that affect their economic growth, the development of their commercial potentials and the expansion of their abilities in the field of trade.
Agreed charges and competitive rates are growing at a fast rate in western Canada as a whole but they are naturally being applied to those movements where alternative forms of transport offer serious competition to the railways. Saskatoon is too far from the west coast to share the advantages of sea transport via Vancouver, which has brought about some relief in freight rates in British Columbia and Alberta. Rail competition through the United States has led to some agreed charges for centres near the international border but Saskatoon is too far north to benefit from these.
The only effective competition with the railways as far as Saskatoon is concerned is highway transportation and load limits on the highways in the province of Saskatchewan are so low as to prevent this being an effective force. Cities on the trans-Canada highway to the south and others in Alberta and Manitoba where weight limits are higher have benefited considerably from agreed charges resulting from highway competition. Thus, while agreed charges are rapidly bringing lower transport costs to western Canada as a whole, Saskatoon is not sharing these benefits because it is poorly placed for service from competing forms of transport.
The development of agreed charges and competitive rates has operated to the disadvantage of Saskatoon in that most other major cities in western Canada have received a competitive advantage in the form of lower transport costs. Already this means that both producers and consumers in Saskatoon face higher costs than in other prairie cities, but its most important impact is on the future development of our city.

Saskatoon is naturally situated so as to become a major centre for the planned development of mineral resources in the northern part of the province. The existing freight rate differentials between Regina and Saskatoon for movements to and from eastern Canada and the west coast mean that any industry locating in Saskatoon faces severe disadvantages vis-a-vis locating, for example, in Regina. Thus, while geographic and economic consideration would naturally lead to the rapid development of Saskatoon as a manufacturing centre, the present freight rate structure is a severe handicap which threatens to slow down the development of Saskatoon and with it the prosperity of the whole of the province and, indeed, the success of plans to develop the northern areas will be handicapped with the handicapping of Saskatoon. This type of effect which results from a system of agreed and competitive charges is most undesirable from our viewpoint.
It was not intended originally and it certainly was not foreseen but it does none the less suggest that a critical reappraisal of the whole system of competitive freight rates is urgently needed. This problem, which is a very real one as far as Saskatoon is concerned, is repeated in other centres throughout Canada facing similar difficulties. An industrial centre does not benefit from low cost highway transportation until it is developed to a considerable extent unless it happens to lie on an existing route. It does not benefit from agreed charges until it has effective competition, and thus the development of new centres on which we rely so much for the expansion of the Canadian economy, particularly in the north, is hampered by the fact that the present freight rate structure gives substantial competitive advantages to existing industrial centres.
It is argued that the basis of agreed charges is sound and it is also argued that there are sound reasons against extending the lower rates of agreed charges to all movements, including those where no effective competition exists. Perhaps both these arguments taken independently could be used to justify the lower charges for most centres and the higher charges for Saskatoon respectively, but I do not agree. When they are used together to justify the existing differential they are unsound as further considerations become important. Professor Winch of the University of Saskatchewan has given a hypothetical example of this situation. He says:
A new industrial plant planning to develop mineral resources is considering its location. Unless it can pay its full costs, including transport costs, it is not a sound proposition ... If rail were the only means of transport and rail rates were consistent on a mileage basis, geographic and other considerations would dictate that it settle in Saskatoon. But if it settles in Regina it would have
Supply-Trade and Commerce
the advantage of lower highway transport costs. It is therefore offered an agreed charge for Regina but not for Saskatoon. It settles in Regina and ships by rail. The net effect is that the industry uses rail transport whether it settles in Saskatoon or Regina, and on the basis of rail and other costs Saskatoon is the preferable location. Yet the industry is forced into locating in Regina because of the existence of highway transport which it will never use. Clearly there is something wrong with a railway system which brings this about, and it is typical of the distortion which the present system will inflict on the rapid industrial development planned for Canada in the future.
The solution is to recognize that the principle of agreed charges is sound, but that it has much wider application than is at present realized. The essential position in the above example is that the agreed charge for Regina is a competing form of transport with the standard rate for Saskatoon and therefore justifies an agreed charge for Saskatoon. But the future of Canada, and particularly of the prairie provinces rests on new industrial development, and the industry with the most flexible location is that which is not yet built. In other words new industrial settlement is the one problem which the present rate structure ignores, and unwittingly impedes, yet it is one vital to the future economy of Saskatchewan, and indeed to the whole of Canada. One of the most important undesirable effects is that of industrial location, and this effect constitutes a severe problem for the whole future of the city of Saskatoon.
I must say that in this connection I am indebted to the board of trade of the city of Saskatoon, the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix and Professor D. M. Winch of the University of Saskatchewan and others who have put effort, time and research into the exposition of this particular problem.
I should like also to refer briefly to another aspect of the trading problem of the west. Here I refer to the use of the port of Churchill as a port for the western provinces. The Hudson bay route association in their annual presentation to the cabinet this spring advocated increased grain storage in the port of Churchill. They suggested on different occasions that increasing the storage facilities there by five million bushels would be of real assistance in the development of this port. They have suggested that more loading berths are necessary. The suggestion they make is that perhaps three more berths are necessary in addition to the ones already located at Churchill. They point out that two only would be required if at least one tie-up wharf for advanced customs inspection was otherwise granted.
There is the problem of the right to ship grain and potash through Churchill from C.P.R. points. Saskatoon has a rapidly developing industry in the industry of potash production. Saskatoon has now come to be rightly called the potash centre of the world. The potash deposits around Saskatoon and in the province of Saskatchewan as a whole are extensive; the markets for potash are very considerable. In order to aid in the
