Supply-Trade and Commerce further expansion of this potash industry it is necessary that consideration be given to making a proper reduction in freight charges through the port of Churchill over the railway in order that the potash producing companies may sell their products in the southern states, for example, and in South America, using the port of Churchill, the Hudson bay railway and the maritime transportation facilities. I am assured that were suitable freight rates granted on the railway, potash from Saskatoon could be placed in the southern United States, using maritime transportation facilities from Churchill, at a competitive rate with United States potash.
I will not deal at this time with the grain car demurrage rates at Churchill except to say that so far as that phase of this particular problem affects the rates at the opening of the season they should be made to equate with those rates charged at Fort William. By the suggestions that I have mentioned tonight the economy of the city of Saskatoon, the surrounding area and the economy of the province as a whole could be significantly and materially improved.

Mr. Chairman, we all realize the importance of export trade to our Canadian economy. I think we all realize that export trade does not come to Canada automatically. In the majority of cases it is essential for the companies of our country and for the government of this country to put on a selling campaign. In view of the present situation in the export field and the growing need for expanding trade for Canada, I sometimes wonder whether the minister or any of the officials of his department have any knowledge of the number of companies in Canada, in particular the large companies of Canada, which have not and are not now putting on any selling campaign and are not trying to get markets outside of Canada because of the fact that they are controlled by parent companies in other countries, and are not permitted, because of that control, to have the temerity to seek markets outside the borders of Canada. I need not make reference at all to the incident of over a year ago where a Canadian car manufacturer was not allowed to sell to the southeast Asian market because of control by a foreign company. We all remember that very well. Of more recent date, we all remember the situation in which the Aluminum Company of Canada declined to make a sale to China, not because they did not have the authority but because they did not want to take a chance of antagonizing their market in the United States in any way.
Now, as a result of incidents of that nature I think it is a reasonable question to ask


how far policies of this type extend to the detriment of Canadian companies and, of necessity therefore, to the detriment of fuller employment in this country. About three years ago an export-import company in British Columbia was interested in finding out if a large number of companies in Canada were interested in exporting to Asian countries, so they wrote a series of letters to varying types of manufacturers across Canada. This company was surprised to receive replies, in a great many instances, not from the Canadian companies interested in these matters but from the parent companies in the United States conveying the information that the Canadian companies were not permitted to deal with production and export outside of the boundaries of Canada. This subject was dealt with wholly and solely by the parent company in the United States.
You will remember, Mr. Chairman, that when the aluminum company declined to make an export to the mainland of China I took up the matter in this house and the newspapers of our country were kind enough to make some mention of that fact. As a result of that I received a letter from this export-import company in which they told me of their experience of some 2J or 3 years ago. In this letter, which I have here, they give excerpts from the replies received from some of these companies. In order to illustrate how far-reaching this control is, I should like to give the committee a number of the excerpts from this letter. There is an excerpt from a letter from Canada Sandpapers Limited, Preston, Ontario, datel February 15, 1956, which reads as follows:
At the moment it would be impossible for us to ship any goods to China, for we are affiliated with a U.S.A. concern, and with the current U.S.A. state department policy, this precludes our shipping any goods to the iron curtain countries.
Here is an excerpt from a letter from Chain-Belt (Canada) Ltd., Willowdale, Ontario, dated February 27, 1956:
All the export business of Chain-Belt Company and Chain-Belt (Canada) Limited is carried on through our export department in Chain-Belt Company, Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
The third excerpt is from a letter from Garlock Packing Company, Pallmyra, New York, dated March 12, 1956:
This refers to your letter of March 5, addressed to our Canadian subsidiary, Toronto. As the latter does not engage in any export operation, at present our business is necessarily restricted to Hong Kong and Taiwan.
This excerpt is from a letter from Canadian Allis-Chalmers Limited, Lachine, Quebec, dated March 12, 1956:

Your offer to represent our company in China has been noted with interest. Canadian Allis-Chalmers is a wholly owned subsidiary of Ailis-Chalmers Manufacturing Company, Milwaukee, Wisconsin. All of our export negotiations are handled through Mr. P. Dietz, manager, export department, industries group, Allis-Chalmers Manufacturing Company, Milwaukee, Wisconsin.
The next letter is from United States Rubber, International, Rockefeller Centre, New York city, dated March 14, 1956:
Your letter of March 6 to Dominion Rubber Company Limited, Montreal, has been referred to me. As Dominion Rubber Company is one of our subsidiaries, we handle any export business that might be developed through Canadian organizations.
Then there is a letter from Jones & Laugh-lin Steel Corporation, New York city, dated March 22, 1956:
Your letter of March 13 addressed to our company in Toronto has been referred to this office for acknowledgment and reply, since all matters pertaining to export are handled here.
I shall just give one more example, although I have plenty more. This letter is from Johns-Manville International, New York city, dated March 29, 1956:
Your letter March 6 addressed to Canadian Johns-Manville Company Limited has been referred to this division, since all overseas matters are our responsibility.
We thank you for your offering to assist us in sales in the Chinese market but regret that we cannot accept your kind offer.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that we in this house have a responsibility to try to find out just how widespread is this control of Canadian companies by parent companies in the United States. We should ascertain to what extent they are restricted in their desire or their potentiality for employing Canadian labour working on our Canadian resources, and their freedom to export to any market to which we have any opportunity or desire to export. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that this is not only an important matter but a very serious one. I believe that we can look upon it as a very disturbing situation. There must be some foreboding about Canadian companies, and therefore Canadian workers, being not only under the control of parent companies outside this country but also dependent upon the whims and policies of a government of another country.
I should like to ask the minister if any consideration has been given to finding out how widespread this control is with regard to exports from Canadian companies. If it is as widespread as is indicated by even the excerpts which I have placed on the record, I wonder whether any consideration is being given to establishing the necessary policy, taking the necessary steps to introduce legislation to guarantee that we have control of
Supply-Trade and Commerce our own resources, our own export policies, without domination from outside.

The fundamental source of income, Mr. Chairman, in our particular part of the world is the pulp and paper industry and the newsprint aspect of it. One of the most disturbing things about the newsprint and pulp and paper industries has been the fact that its percentage share of its main market in the United States has been going down in relation to the expansion of that market and in relation to the expansion of United States production. Since pulp and paper products are the largest single item of export trade, being much more important even than uranium that was mentioned by the Leader of the Opposition, it seems to many of us that the position in which this industry is and its trend toward having a lessened share of the United States market, and of course the world market, is perhaps the most disturbing thing on the economic horizon.
The committee on mines, forests and waters of this house was so greatly interested in this particular point that it brought before it a number of witnesses, including the president of one of the pulp and paper organizations. I refer to Mr. D. W. Ambridge, head of the Abitibi corporation. I wanted to bring to the minister's attention, if he missed it, some of the points that were made by Mr. Ambridge. I should like to qualify, before I give this point, that while I agree with this particular aspect of Mr. Ambridge's evidence there was some of it with which I disagreed. But after reviewing, through questions, the situation that he had seen in Brazil where Canadian firms were not able to compete with Swedish firms because of Swedish government facilities in dealing with Brazilian currency, Mr. Ambridge went on to say this:
The Canadians have about as much chance of selling anything in Brazil as a snowbaU in hell. You cannot do it because there are too many of these arrangements around. We have nothing like that.
Later on Mr. Payne of the committee asked him this question:
Are you in an way satisfied, even in an indirect way, that help is provided to your industry in the search for new markets, through a government agency? Is there such help or is there not?
I should like to point out that Mr. Payne is a member of the minister's party and that the very way in which he phrased the question suggests that he had some concern as to whether this help was available. Mr. Ambridge's answer was:
Not that I know of. The only thing I might name as being of help to us is that the government does provide statistics, through the commercial councillors at the various embassies, legations

Supply-Trade and Commerce
and what-have-you. I think probably we in our newsprint association have the most complete and accurate statistics of anyone in the world.
I am sure Mr. Ambridge is referring to his own product.
Most of those figures overseas come from our commercial councillors in those places. They are helping us in that way.
Mr. Payne came back:
Is there any method you might suggest by which assistance could be given of a practical nature?
I like to see this example of a Conservative member searching for ways of improving the service of this government. Mr. Ambridge came back in reply to this question and said:
I certainly think that the government should give some very serious study to the question of how we are going to finance exports, because this business of cash on the barrelhead is absolute nonsense; it is out of date. We cannot compete. We say, put the money, the American dollars, on the table before we will ship anything. That is crazy. We should certainly have some government body or-I hate to say-committee. You know what they say about a committee. They say a camel is an animal which looks as if it had been put together by a committee.
This led to our turning a bit astray and then we came back and Mr. Ambridge went on to say this:
I think the first thing to do is to get a change of attitude. I do not know who is responsible for this. However, for many years in the Canadian government, the general idea has been that we are not going to get ourselves involved, in extending credit. We are not going to get ourselves involved in barter deals. We are not going to do a damned thing, except take the money when they have it for the products they have to sell. I think that whole attitude might have been valid in the first decade after the war. Since then, it is not valid. We have to face the powerful competition all around the world and we cannot deal with it in any such primitive manner as that. It is primitive.
The business of just going to the market and selling and getting American dollars in New York, is primitive, compared to our competitors.
That is fairly strong stuff and from a free enterpriser like Mr. Ambridge it is very strong when he wants the government to get into this particular field. One of the things I notice is that when anyone ever quotes a Globe and Mail editorial in this chamber there is a tendency to say "That good friend of the government". One of the points that I am almost willing to make, following the Globe and Mail editorial policy in recent months, is that it is no longer a good friend of this government. I think this particular editorial gives an indication as to why that is the case. This is from the Globe and Mail of May 21 and it refers to what Mr. Ambridge said. It states:
The president of Abltibi Power and Paper Company, Mr. D. W. Ambridge, is the latest executive to complain about this dangerous lack of foresight.

It goes on to quote a short extract from what I have already read. Then the Globe and Mail editorial goes on to state as follows:
The government at present has no facilities for granting credit to foreign customers. The limit of its assistance is to insure the sales of Canadian exporters so that the exporters may collect up to 85 per cent of the value of the order if the buyer cannot pay. This service is handled by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, a crown corporation which in the past five years has made a profit of $136,000.
There is nothing in this country remotely similar to the export-import bank of the United States, a government agency which for 25 years has loaned money to foreign buyers for purchases of American goods and services.
Then the editorial goes on to point out that the dominion government in those good old Liberal days was not always so aloof to this problem; that between 1945 and 1948 it extended credit worth some $750 millions. It goes on to say that that program was a courageous step. Then it goes on to lament that really this government has not done much about it and has not given any indication that it is going to get into this extremely important field. The concluding paragraph states as follows:
The important thing is to establish credit facilities now, before it is too late. They will be of no value when our customers have gone for good.
The problem of the pulp and paper industry is much larger than just a question of exports. There is the question of competition. I hope the minister will do a bit of reading on the competition we are getting from southern pine and from the increased use of hardwoods in the lake states and in the New England states. All this is leading to more and more investment and development by United States manufacturers to look after their own domestic market and our share is going down. The main point is that we still have tremendous forest resources that, on a sustained yield basis, we can exploit, but we are not getting any of that. I do not know whether the minister is aware that there are pulp and paper companies in the constituency of the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River which for a long time have been trying to make up their mind about putting a pulp mill into the Sioux Lookout region. For some reason they always back out. These various companies have been delaying for years now. This has tended to be a pattern in the past 10 years. We are getting expansion in plant of mills that are already established but we just cannot seem to get new ones in, especially in the eastern interior and in the boreal forests where we are close to markets.
I am not suggesting this whole pattern is part of the minister's responsibility or interest. But one of the claims that is getting everyone exercised in connection with the pulp and

paper business is that this government or the federal government does not give leadership in financing or credit facilities for this industry in world markets. One of the other things they claim, of course, is that it overtaxes the industry. With all the informational sources that the Minister of Finance and Minister of Trade and Commerce have I think they should be able to come up with some suggestion that would help out this particular industry which at the present time and for many recent months has been producing below capacity.
One of the difficulties, Mr. Chairman, in ever making remarks when the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce are before the committee is that he has such a wonderful capacity of sitting there and shaking his head or giving little smiles to indicate that he feels that what is being said is nonsense.

No; on the contrary. I object to that remark, Mr. Chairman. I was shaking my head on getting a report from my friend to the effect that just a few minutes previously the hon. member read into the record part of the proceedings of a committee that has not yet reported to the house and he is completely out of order. That is why I was shaking my head at it.
I wish you had raised the point.
I would have done so if I had known that the committee had not reported.

I did not realize I was out of order. I could have managed it anyway because Mr. Ambridge's words have been reported very extensively in the press and in the trade magazines. I think I could have managed it but I apologize if I have broken the rule.
One of the points I want to make more seriously than any other point I have ever made in this House of Commons is that the pulp and paper situation in Canada is extremely serious, and if this industry does not pick up our part of the country can almost figure on packing up for a while. I have not exactly a lack of confidence in the particular region, but if pulp and paper does not prosper our region does not prosper. I can point out to the minister that we have had the shipyards closed down in that particular area. The third largest airplane manufacturing plant in Canada is in danger of closing up. We just are not getting secondary industry development, even of a minor character, and if pulp and paper gets into deep trouble in the next couple
Supply-Trade and Commerce of years we will be in a situation comparable, I suppose, to some of the have-not provinces down in the eastern part of Canada. It is about time the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Finance did some serious thinking on this particular problem, or at least gave us the assurance that the people in the industry and the unions who are crying calamity should not be crying calamity.
One of the other points I want to touch on deals with the much mooted small business aspect of this government's policy. One of the largest sources of support for this government in past elections, it seemed to me, was from many of the people in the small manufacturing businesses and I think one of the most appealing aspects the government put forward in its election campaigns was a strong indication that it would help small business. Without going into too much detail the minister has now had two years to get some kind of program under way. One of the great examples in this particular regard is the small loans administration in the United States which, not in a major way but in a minor fashion, has been doing what is considered to be very successful work in the United States for a long time. I would like the minister to confirm that it did not take the United States government two years after it got the idea to commence that particular administration. The United States government got it going very quickly and with a certain sense of urgency.
One of the prime problems in Canada today in a political sense is to try to determine whether the small type of business has a future and whether we should try to preserve it in the face of the build-up of the huge national corporations, or corporations working in a regional sense. They can very soon put small business out of the way. It often seems that small businesses in the present trend have a very bleak future. I had assumed from the stand taken by the government and the minister that it had been decided that small businesses were worthwhile and that the encouragement of small businesses and small manufacturers was very important. But so far all we have had is an indication that there is a senior official who is interested in the problem and that a certain amount of research has been done; that this bureau, or whatever it is, will be prepared to assist small business in an informational sense. But I think they want more than that.
The periodical or brochure which was put out by the department, "The Techniques of Export Trade", is an excellent thing on an informational basis. One of the things, however, which is missing in it is any indication of extended government credit facilities that

Supply-Trade and Commerce the Globe and Mail and Mr. Ambridge called for. I am sure the minister and his assistants in this small business field will be able to turn out just as good a brochure advising the small businessmen how to take care of themselves.
However, I think the minister does recognize that they want more than that. They want a loans administration for small businesses and manufacturers. I cannot see why the example of the United States has not been some encouragement to the minister, and I would like him to give us at some time during his estimates an analysis of why it has not been an encouragement to him to get into this thing. He might at the same time tell us why the example of this United States export-import bank has not been any stimulus to him. It seems to me it is one of the great ironies that the United States, which is usually considered a great free enterprise nation, should be the one that in these particular fields can give our country which has been labelled much less enterprising than the United States such leads or indications of government leadership and initiative. I would hope that in these two fields, and especially in relation to the predicament in the pulp and paper industry at the present time, we will hear more from the minister before his estimates are through.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the minister has consented to allow this item to stand eventually if it appeals to the members of the committee to proceed to other individual and specific items. I want to assure the minister that on that account I am not going to ramble unduly or deal with matters which I do not think specially appropriate to this administration item. I would be very glad to deal with some of the matters we heard about today such as the diversion of trade, the United States conference in January, the 1959 capital investment intentions, of course, and a few matters of that kind. But I cannot find any other appropriate place to say a few words and ask a few questions of the minister with respect to the small business section referred to in the annual report. More than that, it was, of course, given a great deal of prominence, as the minister knows, in both the 1957 and 1958 election campaigns. I think the people of Canada have been led to believe that the government would have moved much further under a new government and something much more tangible would have been done with respect to aid to small business than we yet see either in referring to the report or in the remarks which have been made so far in this debate by the minister. In fact, I think he has made no reference to small business.

Just to indicate that I think I am on pretty sound ground in this respect in outlining what I think is the public opinion with respect to it, these are some of the strong statements which were made by the leader of the Conservative party in 1957 and 1958. I have here some quotations from the Prime Minister. In the last election he said that only minor tax concessions had been made; but he indicated there would be greater assistance. We know that the recent budget actually increased taxes rather than reduced them. Then at Cornwall on February 24, 1958, he said that small business was crucified by the Liberal policy of tight money. I do not need to elaborate on that, but that surely gives even the small group in this chamber tonight a fairly good opportunity for a hearty laugh. Then in starting this campaign at Campbell-ton, New Brunswick, on May 4, 1957 he said:
We intend to do something to assist small business in this country. They find themselves today caught, irretrievably caught, in a situation where they cannot survive.
That was more than two years ago.
We believe the time has come to provide very much alter the fashion of the federal government of the United States.
About six months after this government took office the United States government very considerably widened the availability of loans to small businesses in that country; that is about 18 months ago. I would hope that before we pass the item the Minister of Trade and Commerce will tell us what progress has been made with this particular small business section that has been set up in his department with much fanfare and flurry. May I say that I thought the assistant deputy minister appointed to take charge of this section was very quick to make public policy statements after assuming office, statements which, I thought, should more properly have come from the minister or from the government. But I have watched the papers carefully since, and a number of months have elapsed during which there has been a singular silence about the activities of this particular section, and I hope we shall hear more about it now.

Mr. Chairman, when I was speaking earlier this afternoon the elapse of time allocated to me interrupted a point I was seeking to make concerning the sale of surplus farm products in the export markets of the world at prices well below the cost to the Canadian taxpayer, and I referred the hon. gentleman to two answers to questions given in Hansard indicating particular sales by way of example. One of the sales to which I referred at the point of time when my argument was curtailed was the problem which arose in connection with the export of surplus dried skim milk for feed

purposes to Denmark at a price of the order of something like one-fifth of its cost to the Canadian taxpayer, and I pointed out that one of the implications, in a trade way, of that kind of action was that we were directly subsidizing a competitor in a market in which we were seeking to sell, and I referred particularly to the United Kingdom market.
Now I want to make further reference to another question and answer as it appears in Hansard of June 22, 1959, at page 4993. In reply to a question of mine addressed to the Minister of Agriculture concerning the sale of surplus canned pork by the Canadian government to Czechoslovakia, the minister confirmed that there had been such a sale, and I will read part of his answer:
We have been negotiating with several European countries for some time in an effort to dispose of some of the surplus pork which the stabilization board has held, and particularly from the point of view of attempting to get back into the European market, as far as pork and other agricultural products are concerned.
Then the minister went on to explain that there had been a sale of some 2,200,000 pounds, and he referred to it as being in the nature of a trial shipment and expressed the hope that we should be able to sell in constantly increasing quantities pork and other agricultural products in the European market.
That is a hope which I think everyone will wish to see fulfilled, but what I want to make clear is this: the implications of this policy are manifold. With regard to the example I have just quoted, the minister did not state the price at which the pork was sold, but I understand from outside publications that it represented a loss of the order of nine cents or slightly more a pound. I have not been able to verify that figure as yet, and the minister can correct me if it is wrong. At any rate, on this one product alone there is a surplus of canned and frozen pork of the order of 100 million pounds at the present time, so the loss to the taxpayer would be of the order of $10 million if the figure I have given is correct or substantially correct. That, indeed, is an important item when we bear in mind that we already have a substantial budgetary deficit. So there is this implication of the loss to the taxpayer. And the matter does not end there.
There has been a great deal of debate in this house on the question of the budgetary and financial policy of the government, and I do not wish to enter upon this argument during a discussion of these estimates, but I would point out that one cause of increasing the interest rate in this country is, undoubtedly, the large deficit. This kind of policy contributes to that deficit, and the
Supply-Trade and Commerce deficit, in turn, contributes to increasing interest rates which makes it harder for exporters, manufacturers and producers who are engaged in the export trade to borrow money. It makes it more costly for them to develop their export business, and this in turn increases the cost of our exports and makes it harder for them to compete. In other words, the effect of this policy of disposing of surplus farm products as far as the export market is concerned is to take us in a vicious circle in which, in some cases, the continuation of such policy for these exports tends to destroy the possibility of continuing our normal exports.
There is yet another aspect of the matter. We have had some reason to complain about the farm surplus disposal policy of the United States because we felt that they have been interfering with our markets, and always in earlier years when we made complaints of this kind, we were able to argue with considerable force and put forward a very strong case. We ourselves are now dumping the surplus farm products on world markets at below cost and doing the very things of which we were complaining with regard to the operations of another country. For these reasons I should like the minister to deal fully with this subject and explain the precise nature of our policy in so far as it concerns the disposal of these products outside Canada. I have sought in putting this forward to confine my remarks to the trade aspects of this matter. I appreciate, of course, the attempt which is being made to keep up the level of farm incomes, but I suggest that this is not the best way in which farm incomes can be supported and that there are other ways of dealing with the farm income aspect of the problem.
There is one other question I wish to direct to the minister. His colleague the Minister of Agriculture, in giving the answer to which I have referred, spoke of using this shipment as an attempt to get back into the European market as far as pork and other agricultural products are concerned, and then he spoke of this being in the nature of a trial shipment. I should like to ask the minister if he would elaborate on that part of the answer by telling the committee precisely what is being done and what the government has in mind in its effort to get back into the European markets for agricultural products. Are we to seek to get into those markets by having the Canadian taxpayer subsidize these exports? Is that the new attempt that is being made, or the new policy? If not, what is the policy and on what lines is the government endeavouring to work it out?

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The market prices of these various products in the European market would seem to indicate that our agricultural products are much higher in price than those coming from other competitive areas. We have only to refer to the comparative prices of New Zealand dairy products and our own in the London market and the comparative prices of Danish bacon and our own in the London market. Would the minister indicate to the house just what this new policy was to which the Minister of Agriculture referred and how is it to be carried out? Does it involve a new principle of subsidizing exports, which we have not embarked on hitherto and which even in this case was only an incidental by-product of what happened with 1'egard to the particular transaction? Just what is involved in the matter?

Trade commissioner service-
381.	Administration and operation, $3,747,293.
Would the minister deal briefly with the increase in this item?
There is a slight increase in money and in staff too.
This has to do with the trade commissioner service. The increase amounts to $277,366 and the increase in the staff is seven.
Is there any significant addition to the countries we are represented in or is that for the first year of change handled by the unallocated item that is shown on page 476?
An office was opened in Ankara and we anticipate other new positions during the course of this year and have made allowance therefor.
Were any offices closed?
No, no offices have been closed.
Would the minister give consideration to increasing the service in the United States with a view to seeking the sale of more of our manufactured products in that country?

That is a good point which is really worthy of consideration. We have seven offices there now. I had the pleasure of visiting the one at New York, the one at Chicago and the one at Boston during the last year or so and I was very much impressed with the work that is being done by our trade commissioner service in these places. I also talked to the other trade commissioners stationed elsewhere in the United States. They have been doing some very impressive work in interesting Americans in Canada and in purchasing from Canada.
Just a little while ago I was at the trade fair we held in Boston. It was a good trade fair, was well attended and the exhibits by Canadian businessmen were very good. Last fall I attended a meeting at Chicago organized by the Canadian-American committee of the chamber of commerce of that city. There was a large attendance and a great deal of interest in the problems affecting trade between our two countries. It is noteworthy that that area of the United States is the greatest importer of goods from Canada and the largest exporter, by areas in the United States, to Canada. It is also the area from which a great deal of capital has flowed into Canada and from which subsidiaries have been set up in our country. I found it s very stimulating and interesting experience. I was encouraged by that activity and by the work of our officials in Chicago in getting Americans interested in our country. The results of that work show in a place like Chicago where there has been intense activity as between our two countries.

The trade fair at Boston and the other work being done there will be helpful too. Other areas of the United States that are not as close to Canada naturally have not been affected to the same extent.
My hon. friend's suggestion that we might perhaps extend our trade commissioner service in the United States is something that is well worth considering because trade between our two countries is developing and we want to do everything in our power to encourage the import into the United States of Canadian manufactured products as well as the raw materials which are going there now. I thank the hon. member for drawing the attention of the committee to that particular aspect.

Because many Canadian manufacturing companies are comparatively small they are not aware of the export potential that is possibly available to them. If they could obtain an export market in addition to the market they supply at the present time in Canada, it would tend to permit them to lower their costs. I would feel that is particularly true of exports to the United States in a way that it is possibly not true of exports to certain other foreign countries because many Canadian companies are not large enough to have the facilities for handling normal export trade, but could handle export trade to the United States because of similar trade practices. These smaller firms just have not got the facilities and are not thinking about export, and the trade commissioner service may be able to assist them to increase our exports to the United States if we give more attention at this time to extending their activities, whether by opening new offices in additional areas of the United States or supporting the present offices with expanded services and staff.
This is well worth following up rather closely because, it seems to me, our exporters have a constant problem of operating in a comparatively high cost economy. It is going to be a continuing problem and anything that can be done to get export markets for many of these manufacturing companies not only will be a good thing from the point of view of the business involved but it will be a good thing in that it may help such manufacturers to lower costs both to Canadian consumers and for the export market.

Item agreed to.
382.	Construction or acquisition of buildings, land, equipment and furnishings, $222,000.

Will the minister explain the increase in this item?
Supply-Trade and Commerce

The increase is $61,000. This vote, of course, is for the purpose of providing homes for trade commissioners who are living in areas where in some instances the climate is difficult and in other instances other types of accommodation cannot be rented. Each year an assessment is carried out as to whether or not it is proper to purchase a piece of property or to continue to pay rent. The question of supplying motor cars comes under this item as well. It is rather a modest item, I think. In the long run, where we have been able to purchase rather than to continue to pay out rent, it has been proved to be quite satisfactory.

I had rather direct experience with this particular matter in 1952. It occurred to me that the department was losing a great deal of the efficiency of its staff through lack of proper accommodation in some of the areas of the world where health conditions are not as good as they might be and accommodation is rather difficult to obtain even although for health reasons it is more necessary than in other parts of the world.
I am very glad to see this policy of acquiring properties in such areas is being continued by the present government. I do not know that it is proper for me to name the particular country I had reference to. On that occasion the situation was simply that the trade commissioners and their families were in a state of ill health owing to lack of proper accommodation, bearing in mind the climatic conditions in that area. Can the minister tell us in what countries properties are being acquired.

The committee will be interested in this. We own houses in these locations: Accra, Kingston, Singapore, and two in Tokyo. Then there are houses which are leased and furnished by the department, two in Bombay, one in Colombo, one in Copenhagen, one in Jakarta, one in Hong Kong, one in Karachi, one in Leopoldville and two in New Delhi. Consideration is being given to purchasing accommodation in Teheran and in Paris but that may not occur until next year.

The minister made reference to automobiles acquired by foreign service officers which would be paid for out of this item. Is there a standing regulation with respect to using Canadian manufactured automobiles?
Yes, that is quite right, Canadian manufactured cars.
Item agreed to.
